summary: Defines how the GSS-API can use the Extensible Authentication Protocol as a mechanism. Via the GS2 family from RFC 5801, it also lets SASL applications use EAP.

eli5.summary: It lets programs that already know one way of logging in use another, widely used sign-in system.

subtitle: How applications that speak GSS-API or SASL can sign users in through EAP and a backend AAA server.

tldr.problem: Few GSS-API mechanisms besides Kerberos are in wide use, and GSS-API has no way to separate the server from the mechanism the way EAP and AAA servers do. EAP, meanwhile, supports most common credential types.
tldr.mechanism: The GSS-EAP mechanism wraps an EAP conversation inside GSS-API context tokens made of type-length-value subtokens. EAP channel binding carries the name of the service so the client can check who it is talking to.
tldr.outcome: GSS-API and SASL applications can use federated authentication through RADIUS or Diameter without knowing the EAP method in use. The EAP key is turned into a Kerberos-style key that protects later messages.

today: RFC 7055 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Combine GSS-API and EAP
sections.content:
The GSS-API gives applications a generic way to ask for authentication and per-message protection. The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) authenticates a client to a server, often through a backend AAA server using RADIUS or Diameter. In that setup the access point in the middle does not need to understand the EAP method at all.

The RFC says that apart from Kerberos, few GSS-API mechanisms are in wide use on the Internet, and GSS-API has no facility to separate the server from the mechanism implementation. RFC 7055 combines GSS-API's support for application protocols with EAP and AAA support for common credential types. It is the core mechanism for the ABFAB architecture of federated access for applications. From EAP's view it is a new lower-layer protocol; from the application's view it is a new GSS-API mechanism.

Through the GS2 family in RFC 5801, the same mechanism also lets SASL applications use EAP.
sections.eli5: Many programs know how to ask for a login but only a few kinds. This gives them a way to use a login system that is already common, so they do not each need their own.

sections.title: Roles: Initiator, Acceptor and EAP Server
sections.content:
GSS-API authenticates an initiator to an acceptor, exchanging context tokens that the application delivers reliably and in order. EAP authenticates a peer to an EAP server, optionally through a pass-through authenticator. The EAP peer maps onto the GSS-API initiator. The acceptor role is split between the EAP authenticator and the EAP server.

When a pass-through authenticator is used, most context establishment happens on the EAP server and per-message operations happen on the authenticator. Because the application guarantees delivery, the EAP retransmission timeout MUST be infinite and the EAP layer MUST NOT retransmit a message. If the acceptor cannot get a response from the AAA server, it generates an error at the GSS-API level.

RFC 7055 leaves discovery out of scope; SASL and SPNEGO already describe how mechanisms are found.
sections.eli5: You are the one showing your ID, the door guard checks it, and a records office far away says yes or no. The guard does not need to know how the records office decides.

sections.title: Names and EAP Channel Binding
sections.content:
EAP normally proves a user to a realm, but the peer often does not know which server it is really talking to. GSS-API, in contrast, takes names for both sides. To provide these semantics the mechanism uses EAP channel binding from RFC 6677. The peer sends the acceptor name as channel binding data, the acceptor sends its full name through the AAA protocol, and the EAP server confirms the two agree.

A mechanism name looks like user-or-service/host/service-specifics@realm, with backslash escaping for special characters. The initiator MUST require an EAP method that supports channel binding, and MUST NOT report mutual authentication unless every name element it supplied is in a successful channel binding response.

With RADIUS, the acceptor MUST send its name in attributes 164 (GSS-Acceptor-Service-Name), 165 (Host-Name), 166 (Service-Specifics) and 167 (Realm-Name). Proxies near the acceptor typically verify the hostname, while the EAP server or a proxy it trusts verifies the realm. The EAP server MUST assure the right validation has been done before it returns acceptor names in a successful channel binding response.

This EAP channel binding is a different thing from GSS-API channel binding, which protects against man-in-the-middle attacks when GSS-API runs inside a tunnel.
sections.eli5: It is like a letter that says exactly which building you are visiting. The records office checks that the building really is who it says, so you cannot be sent to a fake one.

sections.title: Choosing the EAP Method
sections.content:
EAP has no way for a server to advertise its methods. The server proposes a preferred method, and a peer that does not accept it replies with a NAK listing the methods it supports. Negotiating at several layers is undesirable, because a client could commit to EAP before learning whether a better non-EAP mechanism is available.

A family of mechanisms, one per EAP method, would keep negotiation in one layer. The RFC rejects that because the acceptor does not know which methods the EAP server implements, and the server used depends on the client's identity. So the design commits to GSS-EAP first and chooses the EAP method afterwards. The two stated costs are that authentication may fail when another method could have succeeded, and that a non-optimal security mechanism may be chosen.
sections.eli5: Picking which way to prove who you are happens after you have already picked the door. That is simple, but sometimes a better door was available.

sections.title: Context Tokens and Subtokens
sections.content:
Context tokens use the framing from RFC 2743. The inner token starts with a 16-bit token ID: 06 01 for initiator to acceptor and 06 02 for acceptor to initiator. The rest is a series of subtokens, each with a four-octet type, a four-octet length and a body. The most significant bit (0x80000000) of the type is the critical bit: a receiver MUST fail context establishment if it sees a critical subtoken it does not understand for the current state. A subtoken type MUST be unique within a token.

The mechanism OID is built from the root 1.3.6.1.5.5.15.1.1 with a Kerberos encryption type number appended. This document defines EAP-AES128, whose OID is 1.3.6.1.5.5.15.1.1.17.

Context establishment runs through three states:

  • Initial: the initiator sends a possibly empty token, optionally with a vendor subtoken (0x0B) or an acceptor name request (0x02). The acceptor MUST include a first EAP request, an identity request.
  • Authenticate: the acceptor carries EAP requests in subtoken 0x80000005 and the initiator carries EAP responses in subtoken 0x80000004, until EAP succeeds or fails.
  • Extensions: after EAP Success, the sides exchange optional flags (0x0C), GSS channel bindings (0x80000006) and a final MIC subtoken (0x8000000D from the initiator, 0x8000000E from the acceptor).

The acceptor may end the exchange at any time with an error subtoken, type 0x80000001, carrying the major status and a GSS-EAP error code.
sections.eli5: The messages are like boxes with labels on them. Each label says what is inside, and some labels say you must open this one or the whole thing stops.

sections.title: Required EAP Method Properties
sections.content:
Because GSS-API options place requirements on EAP security claims, the RFC limits which EAP methods are usable. The mechanism MUST only be used with methods that provide dictionary-attack resistance, typically by tunneling an inner method in TLS. The method MUST support key derivation, mutual authentication and channel binding.

Integrity, confidentiality, sequencing and replay detection MUST be indicated in the output of both context calls regardless of what the application asked for. The PROT_READY service is never available, so per-message protection cannot be used before the context is established. Channel bindings MUST be included in the EAP authentication whether or not mutual authentication was requested.
sections.eli5: Only strong, secret-keeping ways of proving who you are are allowed. A weak one that could be guessed over and over is not accepted.

sections.title: Keys and Per-Message Security
sections.content:
After EAP succeeds, the acceptor provides security services directly. The EAP Master Session Key (MSK) feeds the random-to-key operation of the chosen encryption type to make the GSS-API Master Session Key (GMSK). For aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 that means the first 16 octets of the MSK. If the MSK is too short, authentication MUST fail.

A Context Root Key (CRK) is then derived from the GMSK with the pseudorandom function, using the string rfc4121-gss-eap and a 32-bit counter. The CRK protects the MIC subtokens, using key usage values 60, 61 and 62. Per-message tokens follow RFC 4121, with the CRK treated as the initiator sub-session key, the acceptor sub-session key and the ticket session key. The pseudorandom function from RFC 4402 supports GSS_Pseudo_Random.
sections.eli5: Once you are let in, you and the guard both end up with the same secret code that nobody else has. You use it to seal your messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of the mechanism depends on using and verifying EAP channel binding. The RFC notes that EAP channel binding was in very limited deployment when it was written. Without it, a user could be diverted from one service to another in a phishing attack. For that reason implementations are required to implement and use it.

Layered negotiation can allow bid-down attacks, so the RFC suggests either placing the preferences for all inner-layer mechanisms between two outer-layer ones, or only using this mechanism when it was specifically selected for a service. Every proxy in the AAA chain needs to be trusted to help verify channel bindings and protect key material. RADIUS provides only weak hop-by-hop protection of key material, using MD5 as a stream cipher, while RADIUS over TLS protects it significantly better.
sections.eli5: Everyone between you and the records office has to be honest, and you must check that the building name matches. Otherwise someone could trick you into the wrong one.
